planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall with roots shaded and cool; choose the site with care, since this European native is an extremely vigorous, self-seeding climber that has become a serious woodland and hedgerow weed in parts of the Pacific Northwest and New Zealand.

directions: Traveller's joy is the wild clematis of European hedgerows, a rampant woody climber that scrambles over shrubs, fences, and trees using twining leaf stalks, sometimes reaching the tops of mature trees in its native range. From mid to late summer it opens clusters of small, fragrant, greenish-white flowers lacking true petals, followed in autumn by the fluffy, silvery seed heads of long-persistent plumed achenes that give the plant its common name and provide season-long interest into winter. It tolerates chalky, poor, and alkaline soils better than almost any other clematis and thrives in full sun to light shade, but its vigor and prolific self-seeding mean it is best reserved for a large screen, bank, or naturalized boundary where it has room to roam and can be monitored. Cut back hard in late winter if size needs controlling, since it flowers on the current season's growth.

common_name: Lord Nevill Clematis (Antique Dark Blue Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant deeply with the crown a couple of inches below grade and roots shaded; provide a fence, obelisk, or wall support right away since this is an early large-flowered (pruning Group 2) cultivar that blooms on the previous year's growth.

directions: Raised by the English nursery Thomas Cripps and Son before 1875 and awarded a First Class Certificate by the RHS that same year, this antique large-flowered clematis has survived in cultivation far longer than most of its Victorian contemporaries. In early summer it opens broad, saucer-shaped flowers with six to eight overlapping, wavy-edged, intense dark blue sepals set off by purplish-red anthers, with a lighter second flush possible on new growth later in the season. Because it flowers first on old wood, prune only lightly in late winter, removing dead or weak stems and cutting the rest back to a strong bud rather than hard-pruning the whole plant. Give it rich, well-drained soil with roots kept cool and shaded while the top growth climbs into full sun.

common_name: Mrs. P.B. Truax Clematis (Cold-Hardy Periwinkle-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant with the crown a couple of inches below grade and roots shaded; give it a fence, trellis, or arbor support, since this compact early large-flowered (Group 2) cultivar makes a tidy climber rather than a rampant one.

directions: Raised by the Jackman nursery in 1939, this long-grown large-flowered cultivar bears single periwinkle-blue flowers to about 6 inches across, with a lighter central bar and creamy-white stamens, that fade attractively to light blue as they age. It flowers in a strong flush in late spring to early summer on the previous year's wood, then produces a lighter repeat bloom on new growth in late summer. More compact and comparatively trouble-free than many older large-flowered hybrids, it suits a modest obelisk, pillar, or mailbox trellis as well as a larger fence. Prune lightly in late winter, removing only dead or weak stems to protect the first flush of old-wood flowers.

common_name: Edomurasaki Clematis (Deep Violet-Purple Japanese Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant with the crown a couple of inches below grade and roots kept cool and shaded; give it a sturdy fence, wall, or obelisk to climb, since this vigorous Japanese large-flowered cultivar blooms heavily on old and new wood alike.

directions: Introduced from Japan in 1952, Edomurasaki (meaning roughly 'Edo purple') is a vigorous large-flowered clematis prized for its deep, velvety violet-purple blooms up to 8 inches across, carried in a strong late spring to early summer flush on the previous year's growth followed by a second wave on new wood from late summer into fall. Its rich, saturated color reads darker than many of the better-known blue-purple large-flowered hybrids and holds well without fading in heat. It tolerates sun to fairly shaded positions better than most large-flowered cultivars, making it a useful choice for a partly shaded fence or trellis. Prune lightly in late winter, trimming only dead or weak growth to protect the first flush of flowers on old wood.

common_name: Pangbourne Pink Clematis (Fragrant Non-Climbing Cerise-Pink Bell Clematis)

planting.note: Plant in a mixed border where its wispy, non-climbing stems can lean on nearby perennials or a short twig support; no trellis is needed since it does not twine or climb.

directions: A herbaceous, woody-based selection of the integrifolia group bred by Barry Fretwell and holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit, Pangbourne Pink bears sweetly scented, deep cerise-pink, nodding bell-shaped flowers with paler, creamy centers from early to midsummer. Unlike climbing clematis, it lacks twining leaf stalks and grows as a lax, non-clinging sub-shrub best allowed to sprawl through other border perennials or supported lightly with twiggy pea sticks. Its fluffy, silvery seed heads extend the display into autumn after the flowers fade, and the whole plant can be cut back hard to the base each winter, since it blooms on the current season's growth. Give it moderately fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun or light shade at the front of a mixed border or rock garden edge.
